name: Henryk Sienkiewicz
note: THE ROOM HOLDS QUO VADIS ENTIRE. Rome in the reign of Nero: Petronius, the Arbiter of Elegance, and his nephew Marcus Vinicius, a young tribune back from the wars, who falls for Lygia, a hostage princess raised in a household that has secretly become Christian. Around them the court — Nero singing over the city as it burns, Poppaea, Tigellinus — and below it the first Christians of Rome, Peter and Paul among them, and the arena. Sienkiewicz wrote it in 1895–96 from Tacitus, Suetonius and the Satyricon; it made him famous across the world and was a large part of the Nobel Prize he received in 1905. This is Jeremiah Curtin's English translation of 1896, split by chapter and unedited — the chapters are also what the Amenti Studios cutter reads. The book ends at the little chapel by the Porta Capena that still carries the words Peter is said to have asked on the Appian Way: Quo vadis, Domine? Everything in this room is public domain.
